item.title: FICAC to review Kamikamica court ruling before deciding next legal step
item.description: The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) says it will review the Suva Magistrates Court’s written ruling before deciding whether to pursue any further legal action following the acquittal of former Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica. In a statement, FICAC confirmed the Suva Magistrates Court dismissed the case against Mr Kamikamica after upholding a No Case to Answer applicat
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) says it will review the Suva Magistrates Court’s written ruling before deciding whether to pursue any further legal action following the acquittal of former Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica.

In a statement, FICAC confirmed the Suva Magistrates Court dismissed the case against Mr Kamikamica after upholding a No Case to Answer application on one count of perjury and one count of providing false information to a public servant.

Resident Magistrate Charles Ratakele delivered the ruling yesterday after considering the evidence of Counsel Assisting the Commission of Inquiry, Janet Mason, Member of Parliament Kalaveti Ravu, as well as the agreed facts and documents.

The Court found there was no evidence that Mr Kamikamica made a false statement during the Commission of Inquiry proceedings.

It also ruled that diary entries tendered by Mr Ravu, which were admitted under a hearsay exception, could only establish that the entries were made and not prove the truth of their contents.

The Magistrate further found that Mr Ravu did not explain or elaborate on the diary entries during his oral evidence or provide evidence demonstrating that Mr Kamikamica’s sworn statements were false.

On the charge of providing false information to a public servant, the Court ruled there was no evidence proving that the information supplied by Mr Kamikamica was false.

The Court also noted Ms Mason’s evidence that the issue of Mr Kamikamica’s alleged prior knowledge of the appointment of the FICAC Commissioner was outside the terms of reference of the Commission of Inquiry and was therefore not investigated.

As a result, the Court dismissed both charges and acquitted Mr Kamikamica.

FICAC said it will now examine the Court’s written judgment before determining whether any further legal steps are warranted within the statutory 28-day period for filing an appeal.

Mr Kamikamica was represented by Wylie Clarke and Siddiq Koya, while the prosecution was led by FICAC State Counsels Josann Pene and Setefano Komaibaba.

item.title: Warning notices issued to beggars in Lautoka
item.description: The Lautoka City Council has begun issuing official warning notices to people found begging in public places as part of a joint operation aimed at addressing the growing issue within the city. The initiative, being carried out in partnership with the Fiji Police Force and the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Protection, seeks to ensure public spaces remain safe, accessible and welcoming whil
item.content:encoded:
The Lautoka City Council has begun issuing official warning notices to people found begging in public places as part of a joint operation aimed at addressing the growing issue within the city.

The initiative, being carried out in partnership with the Fiji Police Force and the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Protection, seeks to ensure public spaces remain safe, accessible and welcoming while also connecting vulnerable individuals with the support services they need.

Under the operation, City Rangers are serving warning notices to individuals soliciting alms in public areas. The notices advise that persistent begging and obstructing pedestrian access are offences under the relevant laws and could lead to enforcement action if the behaviour continues.

The Council stressed that the operation is not solely focused on enforcement.

Individuals identified as requiring assistance are being referred to the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Protection, where they can access available welfare programmes and social support services designed to address the underlying causes of their circumstances.

The Council said the collaborative approach balances public safety with compassion by ensuring those in genuine need receive appropriate assistance while maintaining order in public spaces.

Lautoka City Council reaffirmed its commitment to working closely with partner agencies to promote a safer, cleaner and more compassionate environment for residents, businesses and visitors.

item.title: Fiji Airways eyes new Western Sydney route
item.description: Fiji Airways is planning to expand its Australian network with a proposed new service between Nadi and the new Western Sydney International Airport, with flights tentatively scheduled to begin in June 2027. According to aviation schedule tracking website AeroRoutes, the national airline has loaded the new route into its reservation system for the week beginning June 7, 2027. The service is expecte
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Airways is planning to expand its Australian network with a proposed new service between Nadi and the new Western Sydney International Airport, with flights tentatively scheduled to begin in June 2027.

According to aviation schedule tracking website AeroRoutes, the national airline has loaded the new route into its reservation system for the week beginning June 7, 2027. The service is expected to be operated by a 157-seat Boeing 737 MAX 8, although the launch date remains subject to change.

The provisional schedule shows flight FJ991 departing Nadi at 7:55pm and arriving at Western Sydney International at 10:55pm. The return service, FJ990, is scheduled to leave Sydney at 11:55pm and arrive in Nadi at 5:55am the following day.

If confirmed, Fiji Airways would become one of the first international airlines to operate from Western Sydney International Airport, Sydney’s long-awaited second airport, which is due to open before the proposed launch.

Unlike Sydney’s Kingsford Smith Airport, Western Sydney International will operate 24 hours a day without a night-time curfew, allowing airlines greater flexibility in scheduling late-night arrivals and departures.

The proposed Fiji Airways timetable takes advantage of those extended operating hours, with both flights scheduled outside the curfew restrictions that apply at Kingsford Smith.

The new service is expected to strengthen Fiji’s connectivity with Australia, one of the country’s largest tourism markets.

Western Sydney is one of Australia’s fastest-growing regions and is home to a large population with strong demand for international leisure travel.

A direct service to the new airport would provide travellers with easier access to Fiji while reducing the need to travel across Sydney to Kingsford Smith Airport.

Fiji Airways already operates services between Nadi and several Australian cities, including Sydney, Brisbane, Melbourne, Adelaide and Canberra.

The addition of Western Sydney would further expand the airline’s Australian footprint while positioning it to capture growing demand from the rapidly developing western suburbs.

item.title: Inflation holds low despite annual price jump
item.description: Fiji’s average annual inflation remained subdued at 0.2 percent in July 2026, despite consumer prices being 5.7 percent higher than a year ago, according to the latest Consumer Price Index released by the Fiji Bureau of Statistics. The report shows the All Items Consumer Price Index (CPI) fell by 1.1 percent in July, declining from 119.5 in June to 118.2, indicating that prices eased during the mo
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s average annual inflation remained subdued at 0.2 percent in July 2026, despite consumer prices being 5.7 percent higher than a year ago, according to the latest Consumer Price Index released by the Fiji Bureau of Statistics.

The report shows the All Items Consumer Price Index (CPI) fell by 1.1 percent in July, declining from 119.5 in June to 118.2, indicating that prices eased during the month even though they remained significantly above July 2025 levels.

The Bureau uses two measures of inflation. The first compares the average CPI over the previous 12 months with the average over the preceding 12-month period, while the second measures price changes between the same month in consecutive years.

Health recorded the largest monthly increase among major expenditure groups, rising 1.1 percent, driven by higher prices for pharmaceutical products.

Food and non-alcoholic beverages increased by 0.5 percent, reflecting higher prices for bread and cereals, fish and seafood, oils and fats, as well as fruit and vegetables.

Recreation and culture also rose 0.5 percent, with increases in the cost of electronic equipment, information processing devices and newspapers.

Restaurant and hotel prices edged up 0.2 percent, while furnishings and household maintenance recorded a modest 0.1 percent increase.

Education costs remained unchanged during the month.

The largest decline was recorded in the transport division, which fell 6.6 percent, mainly due to lower prices for fuels and lubricants for private vehicles and passenger transport services.

Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels decreased 1.4 percent, driven by lower prices for gas and liquid fuels.

Other categories that recorded price declines included clothing and footwear (-0.4 percent), miscellaneous goods and services (-0.2 percent), communication (-0.1 percent) and alcoholic beverages, tobacco and narcotics (-0.1 percent).

The latest figures suggest that while some essential household items, particularly food and healthcare, continue to experience upward price pressure, falling fuel and transport costs helped ease overall consumer prices during July.

item.title: Sugar review committee heads north
item.description: The Special Committee on the Sugar Industry, chaired by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, will be in the Northern Division on Wednesday and Thursday for consultations with sugarcane farmers and visits to key sugar industry facilities. The committee’s visit will provide farmers with an opportunity to raise concerns and make submissions on the challenges facing the industry and possible measures to se
item.content:encoded:
The Special Committee on the Sugar Industry, chaired by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, will be in the Northern Division on Wednesday and Thursday for consultations with sugarcane farmers and visits to key sugar industry facilities.

The committee’s visit will provide farmers with an opportunity to raise concerns and make submissions on the challenges facing the industry and possible measures to secure its future.

The committee was established by Parliament to undertake a comprehensive review of Fiji’s sugar industry and provide recommendations for its transformation and long-term sustainability.

The other committee members are MP Biman Prasad, Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Tourism and Civil Aviation Viliame Gavoka, MP Manoa Kamikamica, Minister for Sugar Industry Tomasi Tunabuna, Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu, Policing Minister Ioane Naivalurua and Assistant Minister for the Office of the Prime Minister Sakiusa Tubuna.

The committee will begin the day with a debrief at Hotel Takia in Labasa from 9am to 10.15am, followed by morning tea.

From 10.45am to 11.45am, the committee will hold a courtesy meeting with the Commissioner Northern.

After lunch, the delegation will travel to Seaqaqa, with the journey scheduled from 1.15pm to 2pm.

From 2pm to 4pm, the committee will hold a consultation with sugarcane farmers at Sanatan Hall, Seaqaqa, before returning to Labasa at about 4.30pm.

The committee will hold a consultation with sugarcane farmers from the Labasa area from 10am to noon at the Vanua Levu Arya Samaj Hall in Namara.

This will be followed by a tour of the Labasa Sugar Mill from 12.10pm to 1pm.

Lunch will then be hosted by the Commissioner Northern from 1pm to 2pm, before the committee returns to the hotel for rest.

item.title: ‘Flashing light’ that saved six
item.description: AFTER nearly 37 hours adrift at sea with nothing but life jackets and a wooden plank to keep them afloat, the six medical workers from Lau were running out of hope. But as darkness surrounded them, a mysterious flashlight appeared in the distance, a small beam that would eventually guide rescuers to their location.
item.content:encoded:
AFTER nearly 37 hours adrift at sea with nothing but life jackets and a wooden plank to keep them afloat, the six medical workers from Lau were running out of hope.

But as darkness surrounded them, a mysterious flashlight appeared in the distance, a small beam that would eventually guide rescuers to their location.

A faint flashlight beam, impossible to explain given the distance and the rough conditions, pierced through the night, guiding the crew of the Lomaiviti Princess XII towards the missing medical team and ending one of the most intense maritime searches in recent memory.

For Captain Adriano Rabolabiu, the moment was nothing short of divine intervention. Mr Rabolabiu recalled receiving the distressing news that a boat carrying seven people had capsized while travelling in Lau waters, as they were travelling to Vanuavatu in Lau.

His immediate concern was reaching the missing medical workers as quickly as possible. The search began with a series of urgent calls. Mr Rabolabiu said he contacted Lakeba Hospital and was told the medical team had departed after 8pm but had not arrived at their destination by midnight.

He then began checking whether nearby vessels and authorities had been informed.

“There’s a vessel just ahead of us. Have you informed them that they are missing people out at sea?” he recalled asking.

After being told only police had been notified, Mr Rabolabiu said he immediately took action. He contacted the vessel ahead, informed the Republic of Fiji Military Forces, and requested regular updates while the search continued.

The next morning, a message from the Navy appeared to bring relief.

“At 10 o’clock in the morning, he (a crew mate) came running to me. He said, there’s a text from the Navy. They’ve been found in Nayau.”

He rushed to the wheelhouse and checked the message himself. However, as he began making further calls, he realised something was wrong.

The information was later confirmed to be false after a vessel searching the area had been mistaken for the missing boat.

The search continued. Mr Rabolabiu contacted communities across Lau, including Oneata, Olorua and Komo, asking whether anyone had seen signs of the missing team.

Still, there was no news. After reaching Vanuavatu in Lau and unloading passengers and supplies, the captain decided the search would continue.

“We just had the passengers disembark with all their shopping things and their essential items they need for two weeks.

“The building material and the big drums, we left it on board and we took off. Because we were losing daylight.”

He said maritime law requires a ship captain to assist people in distress. At around 3pm, Mr Rabolabiu gathered his crew in the wheelhouse and began coordinating a wider search.

“I then announced to the passengers to help us look. Everyone helped us. They were shining lights because it would reflect on the teams life jackets, for us to spot.”

As the ship moved through the waters searching for any sign of the missing medical workers, Mr Rabolabiu went inside to pray.

“I have a prayer called Divine Mercy — ‘Jesus, I trust in you’. It never failed me and it didn’t fail me.”

Then came the moment that changed the search. From above the vessel, crew members began shouting.

“Light, light, light!” The crew had spotted a flashing light in the darkness.

Mr Rabolabiu immediately contacted Lakeba Hospital to confirm whether the missing team had a flashlight.

“They said no, they had nothing but life jackets and a plank,” he said. For the captain, the circumstances surrounding the light were difficult to explain.

After the rescue, he calculated the distance between where the light was spotted and where the survivors were found.

“It was 2.6 nautical miles. As a ship captain, that was a very unlikely odd. Imagine a torchlight at 2.6 miles, shining through waves like that (rough mounting waves).

“When we came close, right to the end when they were just about 100 metres away, I still couldn’t see them properly because of the waves. But the guys on top could see them.”

It was later learnt that as the crew while out at sea prayed for as long as they can and out of the blue a Toshiba flash light floated towards them allowing them ship and signal at the vessel later.

The rescue operation began at about 7pm. However, getting the exhausted medical workers safely aboard was another challenge.

Mr Rabolabiu said the crew had difficulty deploying the rescue dinghy due to the rough conditions. But eventually, the team was brought safely aboard.

item.title: Rescue shows frontline dedication
item.description: THE rescue of six health workers from Lau waters has highlighted the need to support not only health infrastructure but also the people and systems delivering medical services. Speaking on The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said the incident underscored the dedication of health workers serving communities, particularly in remote areas.
item.content:encoded:
THE rescue of six health workers from Lau waters has highlighted the need to support not only health infrastructure but also the people and systems delivering medical services.

Speaking on The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Australian High Commissioner to Fiji Peter Roberts said the incident underscored the dedication of health workers serving communities, particularly in remote areas.

He said while Australia was working with the Fijian Government to support future health infrastructure, including planning for the redevelopment of the Colonial War Memorial Hospital, effective health services depended on more than buildings.

“At this stage, we’ve supported work on what’s called the clinical services plan,” he said.

“So we have an assessment of what’s actually needed and then on the master plan for what comes after CWM.”

Mr Roberts said the Fijian Government was considering the next steps and Australia remained interested in supporting the project.

“It’s a big project, so I think you’ll probably have lots of people working with you on CWM, but it’s really important.”

“We’ll work on the infrastructure, but we’ll also work with the ministry to support the wraparound of all that.”

He described the rescue of the Lau health workers as “fantastic”, saying it highlighted the importance of frontline workers alongside infrastructure investment.

Mr Roberts said Australia remained keen to support the CWMH project as discussions progressed, noting a development of that scale would require multiple partners

item.title: People First claims FijiFirst political legacy
item.description: THE People First party has officially identified itself as the political successor to the deregistered FijiFirst Party. Speaking at the party launch last Saturday, leader Inia Seruiratu said the party was formed after the deregistration of FijiFirst in July 2023, arguing that the move left thousands of supporters without their chosen political representation.
item.content:encoded:
THE People First party has officially identified itself as the political successor to the deregistered FijiFirst Party.

Speaking at the party launch last Saturday, leader Inia Seruiratu said the party was formed after the deregistration of FijiFirst in July 2023, arguing that the move left thousands of supporters without their chosen political representation.

Mr Seruiratu said former FijiFirst members who remained in Parliament as independents had the freedom to choose their own political paths but decided to remain committed to those who had voted them into office.

“During that critical period, we faced immense pressure, but we stood our ground because of you that voted us in,” he said.

“We refused to compromise the faith you placed in us. We chose to stand firm for Fijians who believe in equality, integrity, respect, and national unity.”

He said those circumstances led to the creation of People First.

Mr Seruiratu also said the party would not release a manifesto before consulting the public, saying community input would shape its policy platform.

He also criticised the current state of governance, saying promises of improved transparency, accountability and higher standards had not been fulfilled.

Mr Seruiratu said People First aimed to offer an alternative built on constitutional principles and a commitment to honesty and collaboration with the public.
